name: Sorghum

project_scope.source_pool: Master Plant Pool rows 1110–1111; Genus Study Index row 149
project_scope.learner_status: Both species are in data/manifest.json as installed learner cards; source-pool and county native decisions remain separate. S. halepense user-directed finished text pass 2026-10-20; rhizome and detailed ligule photos still missing.
project_scope.native_range_guardrail: Both are introduced grasses in Central Texas; they are not counted among confirmed native target-zone taxa. S. bicolor includes cultivated grain/forage forms and escaped shattercane; S. halepense is invasive Johnsongrass.

shared_genus_recognition.look_here_first: Find a true grass node and collar/ligule, then trace one flowering branch to paired spikelets: a larger usually bisexual SESSILE spikelet attached directly to the short axis and a PEDICELLATE companion spikelet on a stalk, often staminate or sterile. This separates Sorghum from lookalike panicle grasses far more reliably than its white leaf midrib alone.
shared_traits: Tall warm-season grasses with broad leaves and prominent midribs, jointed culms, terminal branched panicles and paired spikelets at the end of small racemes.
The fertile sessile spikelet bears a caryopsis enclosed by hardened glumes; the partner pedicellate spikelet may be staminate or functionally sterile.
Panicle shape changes with domestication: broad compact sorghum grain head is common but feral/crop lines can have lax heads; don't mistake cultivar form for a separate species.

terminology.definition: Membrane/hairy boundary on inner collar where leaf blade meets sheath.
Belowground horizontal stem with scale leaves and nodes; Johnsongrass can regenerate from its rhizomes.
Branched flower/seed head; Sorghum has short raceme units at branch tips.
Spikelet directly attached without a stalk, typically fruit-producing in these Sorghum species.
Companion spikelet on a small stalk; may be male or sterile.
Ripe spikelets naturally detach/disarticulate from panicle; wild Johnsongrass shatters much more readily than selected grain sorghum.

shared_genus_recognition.handling: Photograph rhizomes where exposed from maintenance, not by disturbing protected/native plant roots. For invasive Johnsongrass, do not scatter seed or rhizome fragments. Do not sample or feed stressed Sorghum foliage to livestock; cyanogenic glycosides can be hazardous under some conditions.

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Usually cultivated/feral ANNUAL or short-lived perennial, with fibrous roots and no extensive creeping rhizomes
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Robust PERENNIAL with extensive tough scaly rhizomes; emerges in patches from underground stems
species_comparison_matrix.weight: MOST IMPORTANT vegetative split; document exposed rhizome with nodes/scale leaves

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Very variable from dense grain heads to lax shattercane/forage panicles depending on cultivar/escape
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Usually conspicuously open, pyramidal to lanceolate panicle with spreading branches
species_comparison_matrix.weight: FIRST DISTANT CLUE, not taxonomic proof

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Typically broader blades, often 2–10 cm (20–100 mm), especially grain/forage types
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Typically narrower blades ~0.8–4 cm (8–40 mm); broad forms overlap

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Fertile sessile and companion pedicelled spikelet at branch tips; often larger, plump caryopsis in crop forms
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Fertile sessile spikelet ~3.8–6.5 mm long with companion stalked usually staminate spikelet; short spikelet-bearing branchlets

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Cultivated grain types have nonshattering or tardily shedding spikelets, but feral shattercane can readily shatter
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Rachis normally disarticulates readily below sessile spikelets, scattering ripe units

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Grain colors white, reddish, brown and many others; awns vary by cultivar and wild/feral line
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Spikelets often straw/brown/reddish-purple; lemma may be awnless or have short geniculate twisted awn (~0–13 mm)
species_comparison_matrix.weight: LOW; colors and awns cannot distinguish reliably

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Grain crop, planted forage, birdseed/roadside spill or escaped shattercane
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Road edges, disturbed ditches, riparian corridors, turf edges and perennial infestations
species_comparison_matrix.weight: CONTEXT NOT PROOF: feral bicolor can occur on roadsides too

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: whole plant plus collar/ligule and a real culm node
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Confirm a grass and record mature height, blade width and white midrib only as supporting traits.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: basal stem and naturally exposed underground stems
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Thick segmented creeping scaly rhizomes strongly indicate perennial S. halepense; no rhizomes and a fibrous annual clump lean S. bicolor.
Open large loose branched panicle leans halepense; compact densely seeded grain head leans domesticated bicolor, but feral bicolor overlaps.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: single intact spikelet PAIR with mm scale
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Identify pedicelled versus sessile spikelet and the lower vs upper glumes, rachis attachment, awn if any; ensure true Sorghum architecture.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: ripe head still on plant; unforced naturally detached units
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Easy seedhead shattering favors halepense but escaped S. bicolor can shatter; don't shake plants or spread seed to test.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: no underground, flower/fruit evidence or irregular suspected hybrid
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Use Sorghum sp. or S. bicolor/halepense complex as appropriate; photo set incomplete and gene flow/feral line possible.

diagnostic_photo_requirements.show: Side view of intact underground horizontal white/tan segmented rhizome with nodes and buds on halepense; clean fibrous base on bicolor. Photograph roots already exposed by maintenance; avoid scattering fragments.
MM ruler and arrows for sessile fruiting spikelet, pedicel, pedicellate companion, glumes, awn and rachis. Use transmitted macro or dissecting microscope.
Compact domestic bicolor, lax/feral bicolor and open halepense. Three panels explicitly show overlap rather than a false binary.

diagnostic_photo_requirements.role: collar zone ligule and blade widths
diagnostic_photo_requirements.show: Ligule membrane/cilia, sheath, true node, leaf blade with cm scale and pale midrib.
Naturally retained bicolor crop grains versus disarticulated halepense mature branch, with cautious exception for shattercane.
Sorghum companion fully formed pedicellate spikelet versus Sorghastrum pedicellate partner highly reduced/vestigial; include mm macro and count structures.
Johnsongrass perennial patches alongside seeded grain/forage plants; habitat does not identify species alone.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Sorghastrum nutans (Indiangrass; desirable native)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Sorghastrum has long awns and a highly reduced companion pedicelled spikelet (often represented by pedicel); Sorghum halepense has a formed companion spikelet. Check grass florets under magnification before deciding management.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Panicum virgatum (switchgrass; native)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Large open panicles overlap in silhouette but Panicum spikelet architecture lacks Sorghum's characteristic sessile–pedicellate pair.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Zea mays (maize)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Broad grass foliage with white midrib may overlap but distinct terminal staminate tassel and separate ear; not a Sorghum terminal fruiting panicle.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Sorghum almum and bicolor × halepense / feral forms
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Perennial or hybrid forage sorghums can complicate annual-versus-rhizomatous separation. Photograph underground organs and spikelet pairs; expert confirmation if traits conflict.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Setaria spp.
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Foxtail head has conspicuous bristles subtending spikelets; no Sorghum sessile/pedicellate pairing.

scientific_cautions: Both source taxa currently appear as canonical learner species in data/manifest.json. Their original source-pool Curated flag, native range approval and individual photo/diagnostic states must be kept separate from learner installation.
Both are introduced to Central Texas; S. bicolor is African-origin cultivated, S. halepense Eurasian/African-origin introduced invasive. This is not a native-only recommendation.
Domestic S. bicolor may be a nonrhizomatous perennial in frost-free settings, so do not equate 'can resprout' with halepense; belowground creeping rhizomes are the stronger character.
Shattercane is a feral/weedy S. bicolor form with shattering seeds and sometimes open heads. It defeats simplistic panicle and seed-retention shortcuts.
Some sorghum hybrids and forage cultivars cross or show perennial/rhizomatous traits; unresolved hybrids should not be forced into one bin.
Management relevance: removing one Johnson grass shoot is not rhizome eradication; vegetative fragment movement can spread it. This is ID guidance, not a chemical treatment prescription.
Prominent white leaf midrib occurs in multiple grasses and should never be an exclusive ID trait.
Sorghastrum nutans is a desirable native look-alike: require spikelet anatomy before labeling a restored grass invasive.

Both species ALREADY installed in manifest; do NOT duplicate. Update existing cards and genus lesson only, preserve non-native scientific range decisions and old rejected image audit.

look_here_first: SORGHUM crew recognition: actually compare cultivated S. bicolor robust upright crop canes and variable grain panicles with introduced invasive S. halepense true CREEPING segmented rhizomes. Both have large leaves and potentially open heads; confirm original sessile+pedicelled Sorghum spikelet pair under hand lens. Pale midrib and purplish head only supporting cues. Don't call Johnsongrass a native bunchgrass; treat crop shattercane escapes cautiously.
shared_traits: Jointed culms with sheathing leaves, ligules and terminal branched panicles.
At raceme tips, a sessile fruiting spikelet is paired with a pedicellate companion; use a hand lens to confirm both.
Grain sorghum head compactness is shaped by cultivation; some escaped S. bicolor have open, easily shattering heads.
overlap_cautions: Leaf width overlaps: bicolor often ~20–100 mm and halepense often ~8–40 mm; broad halepense and narrow bicolor can confuse.
Open panicles and shattering are not exclusive to Johnsongrass; feral shattercane can have both.
A white midrib, reddish seedheads or awns are not reliable species keys.
Perennial or hybrid forage sorghums can combine traits. If rhizomes and spikelets disagree, record Sorghum sp. and hand off for voucher review.
Both taxa are source-pool comparison names, not canonical species cards; this lesson installs no species or photos.

comparison_cards.title: Johnsongrass versus crop or feral sorghum
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Check segmented creeping rhizomes, then compare paired spikelets and panicle architecture.
comparison_cards.measurements: Typical leaf width ~8–40 mm (halepense) versus ~20–100 mm (bicolor); overlaps substantially.
comparison_cards.caution: Feral shattercane can have loose heads and easily detached seeds; underground organs are stronger evidence.
comparison_cards.photo_role: matched root base, rhizome nodes and whole panicle, all with ruler; needs_photo

comparison_cards.title: Sorghum versus Indiangrass
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Examine the spikelet partner under magnification: a formed stalked companion in Sorghum versus reduced/vestigial partner in Sorghastrum.
comparison_cards.caution: Open panicle silhouette alone can cause native Indiangrass to be mistaken for introduced Johnsongrass.
comparison_cards.photo_role: same-scale dissected spikelet pairs with visible pedicels; needs_photo

comparison_cards.title: Sorghum versus switchgrass and foxtails
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Switchgrass lacks the characteristic sessile/pedicellate Sorghum pair; foxtails have conspicuous bristles below spikelets.
comparison_cards.caution: A broad grass leaf or seedhead color does not identify genus.
comparison_cards.photo_role: matched mature spikelet and head close-ups; needs_photo

visual_comparison.title: SORGHUM — crop sorghum versus Johnsongrass, from head to rhizome
visual_comparison.subtitle: Six existing original source panels retained. Both species now have field lesson status; crop sorghum card additionally links the real Johnsongrass rhizome/collar as explicitly other-species examples.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: HEAD = a clue; PALE MIDRIB = a clue; SEGMENTED SPREADING RHIZOME + true SORGHUM paired spikelets = stronger Johnsongrass evidence. Native Indiangrass is a separate taxon.

items.label: CROP/FORAGE SORGHUM — whole plant with broad blades and flowering panicles
items.image_role: whole stems and open branched panicles with broad leaves
items.caption: Existing Montana whole-shoot photo shows tall stems, broad leaves and branching seed panicles in an uncrowded view. Cultivated bicolor panicles range from dense to open; this photograph is a crop-type example only, not a definitive species key.
items.why_it_matters: Sets the baseline for sorghum versus Johnsongrass: morphology of a whole adult plant before examining reproductive pairs and underground organs.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Source-labelled Matt Lavin Commons photo CC BY-SA 2.0; not an Hays voucher and no rhizome anatomy visible. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.

items.label: JOHNSONGRASS — open purplish panicle
items.image_role: Recognize it — complete reddish open branched terminal Sorghum panicle atop broad-leaved shoot. Purple/red color is a clue only, not a definitive species separator.
items.caption: Texas source-labelled Johnsongrass shoot with broad leaves and airy reddish/purplish panicle. A yellow arrow is ALREADY baked into the original image pointing at the actual flowering head; do not add a second marker. Purple color is a supporting clue, not sufficient for identification.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the more open branched panicle typical of Johnsongrass alongside crop sorghum's variable heads.
items.creator: (c) Annika Lindqvist, some rights reserved (CC BY)
items.photo_status: Physically archived Texas source image, original printed panicle arrow previously pixel-reviewed; no newly imposed overlay. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.

items.label: JOHNSONGRASS — broad blade with pale midrib
items.image_role: Look closer — true bright pale longitudinal central midrib of broad Johnson grass leaf visible on left blade; note white midrib by itself is NOT species diagnostic.
items.caption: A very pale central vein is visible in one broad green blade and already has a yellow printed arrow in the archived image. This helps find the plant in grass stands but several native and cultivated grasses can share a pale midrib.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches the intentionally NON-DIAGNOSTIC early visual clue; crews must go on to collar, rhizome, and spikelet pair.
items.creator: (c) Linda Jo Conn, some rights reserved (CC BY)
items.photo_status: Physically archived source-labelled Texas blade photograph; old printed arrow retained, no new overlay. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.

items.label: JOHNSONGRASS — actual spreading segmented rhizome
items.image_role: Confirm underground structure — pale, jointed creeping rhizome, photographed as one continuous belowground stem with nodes. Some buds are not resolved; compare the joints with nearby true fine roots.
items.caption: Moadeeb's licensed Austin/Texas photo shows a horizontal whitish underground stem with segmentation and attached roots. Trace true stem joints/nodes along the rhizome; individual buds are NOT verified at this image scale. Avoid digging and moving viable invasive pieces except with proper collection protocol.
items.why_it_matters: This is the high-value structural separator: Johnsongrass has persistent creeping rhizomes; typical cultivated S. bicolor lacks this network.
items.creator: Moadeeb
items.photo_status: Original pixel review in archived source metadata supports visible pale jointed rhizome, but measured buds and scale leaves need a further macro. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.

items.label: JOHNSONGRASS — fringed membranous ligule close-up
items.image_role: Look closer — hairy/fringed ligule region where blade meets sheath. Do not label an unmeasured 2–6 mm membrane from this angle; inspect a second collar with blade gently pulled back.
items.caption: A dense whitish hair fringe is visible at the leaf sheath/blade collar. The transparent 2–6 mm membrane itself has not been separately measured from this angle, so mark the broader collar/ligule region only in instructional text, not a numerical arrow.
items.why_it_matters: Provides actual leaf-collar structure instead of another generic full-head photo, without pretending the length was measured.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Original photo pixels previously reviewed in project record; no source-specific arrow to an unmeasured membrane. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.

items.label: JOHNSONGRASS — feathery stigma at reproductive units
items.image_role: Look closer — white-beige plume-like pollen-receiving stigmatic branches emerging near small Sorghum reproductive units. Do not infer one sessile + one pedicellate full pair without clearly visible attachments.
items.caption: The existing printed arrow indicates a pale feathery pollen-receptive STIGMA. It is not a dissected paired-spikelet diagram; the fertile directly attached spikelet and pedicellate companion positions need an intact mature specimen.
items.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a real reproductive organ and shows crews why microscopic attachment checks are more reliable than color or panicle size.
items.creator: (c) Linda Jo Conn, some rights reserved (CC BY)
items.photo_status: Original physically archived Texas photo with existing verified printed stigma arrow; no invented sessile/pedicellate markers. Existing physically archived exact taxon photograph; no new overlay arrows. Existing source photo pixels, attribution, license and modification record retained.
